rp-01.a.text: Before any safeguards are designed, the assessment team scores the warehouse's exposure to fire exactly as the building stands today, with no sprinklers and no controls assumed.
rp-01.a.why: Scoring the environment as it exists prior to any risk management effort is the starting-point measurement — the same fire exposure, once controls are in place, gets a different name.
rp-01.b.text: After sprinklers, fire doors, and a suppression contract are installed, the team scores what fire exposure the warehouse still carries.
rp-01.b.why: What remains once safeguards have already been applied — the gap management is left to accept or treat further — is measured after the fact, never before controls exist.

rp-02.a.text: A ransomware crew has publicly stated it is actively targeting hospitals that run unpatched imaging servers this quarter.
rp-02.a.why: A potential source of harm to an asset — the actor or event capable of causing damage — is what this side names, independent of whether the target has any weakness to exploit.
rp-02.b.text: The hospital's imaging server has been running an unpatched OS build for eleven months, with the vendor's fix sitting unapplied.
rp-02.b.why: The flaw or absence of a safeguard in the asset itself, which a threat could exploit, is the other half — a weakness can exist even with no attacker currently pursuing it.

rp-03.a.text: A disgruntled administrator who left last month has been telling former colleagues he wants to hurt the company, and he knows the payroll database well.
rp-03.a.why: Naming the potential source of harm on its own, before it is combined with how exploitable the target is or what damage would follow, keys this side.
rp-03.b.text: Given that the same administrator's credentials were never revoked and still work on an unmonitored VPN account, the payroll database's likelihood and impact of unauthorized access this quarter is assessed as high.
rp-03.b.why: Combining a threat with the vulnerability it can exploit into a measured likelihood and severity of harm is the calculation this side performs — a threat alone is only one input to it.

rp-04.a.text: Senior management publishes a one-page document stating that all customer data must be encrypted, without naming any algorithm or key length.
rp-04.a.why: A high-level, management-issued statement of intent and scope — mandatory, but silent on implementation detail — is what this side captures; the specifics live one level down.
rp-04.b.text: A companion document mandates AES-256 with a 90-day key rotation for every system that stores customer data.
rp-04.b.why: A specific, compulsory requirement that makes an upstream policy's intent uniformly enforceable across the organization is this side's role — it says exactly what, where the policy only said that.

rp-05.a.text: Every laptop in the fleet must have full-disk encryption switched on before IT hands it to its user, and no team may opt out.
rp-05.a.why: The same control, stated as a compulsory requirement applied uniformly with no discretion left to the implementer, is what defines this side.
rp-05.b.text: A companion document advises switching full-disk encryption on before a laptop is handed over, while noting a team may substitute an equivalent protection where that suits its workflow better.
rp-05.b.why: The identical control, offered as advice with substitution permitted, is the other half — a recommendation that can be adapted locally, never an enforced rule.

rp-06.a.text: The team calculates that a server outage has a single loss expectancy of $40,000 and an annualized rate of occurrence of 0.5, giving an annualized loss expectancy of $20,000.
rp-06.a.why: Assigning real dollar figures derived from mathematical calculation, such as SLE and ARO feeding an ALE, is this side's method.
rp-06.b.text: Unable to price the outage precisely, the same team instead has stakeholders rank it 'high' impact and 'likely' frequency on a workshop scorecard, based on their judgment and experience.
rp-06.b.why: Subjective, scenario-driven ranking using judgment and intuition rather than dollar calculations is the other half of the pair, used when the figures aren't available or precise.
